title: How does a logo change affect brand image? Social media rebranding, with Instagram as the example
excerpt: Instagram's logo change stirred up more feeling online than the app's refresh of its entire interface. It looks like the haters of the update outnumber its fans. Does a small icon really matter that much to using an app? A company's logo and its name are the basic identifiers of any brand — the brand that consumers get used to. Instagram, though, isn't afraid of big changes.
metaTitle: How does a logo change affect brand image? The Instagram rebrand
metaDescription: Instagram's logo change stirred up more feeling online than a whole interface refresh. Does a small icon really matter that much?

runs.text: A company's logo and its name are the basic identifiers of any brand — the brand that consumers get used to. Instagram, though, isn't afraid of big changes. Few people remember that this isn't the platform's first rebrand — early in its life it went by “Burbn”. That name change didn't echo anywhere near as loudly as the latest revolution, in an era when the app belongs to Mark Zuckerberg, who has no qualms about putting extreme new ideas into practice.
Why did Instagram change its logo?

Ian Spalter, Instagram's art director, explains that the logo change is meant to reflect the shifts the platform has been through since it was founded. In its creator's intent, the new flat-design icon points to the trend of instantly photographing everything around us. Now that smartphones are everywhere, it's no longer only about showing off photos online under a filter that styles them as dated, but also about telling stories with those photos. To get there, Spalter used an unusual method to arrive at the new symbol. He asked his colleagues to draw the existing logo in 10 seconds. Most of them managed to sketch a lens and a small black viewfinder, so those elements were kept in the refreshed version. The new logo is more pared back now, symbolic even, which its creator says calls to mind not only traditional cameras but also the smartphones we use day to day to capture moments on a screen. Spalter explains that “the new logo is closer to how people use cameras today”. Most users don't agree with that premise. For opponents of the update, the association with retro photography was exactly what marked the platform out. Beyond that, the excessive simplicity doesn't speak to them — they hold that, unlike the new one, the old logo was detailed and showed off real skill on the designer's part. The internet reacted to the rebrand in a flash. A few examples of the response to the new logo below:
What did the new identity look like?

If we had to call it right now: at first blush, Instagram's rebrand didn't look like a good way to deepen the relationship with its existing users. Users didn't appreciate the show of growth and modernity, but it certainly got their attention. There was no missing word of the new icon while browsing the news online, even for people who don't follow social at all. It's worth adding, though, that users of social channels get used to change remarkably fast — proof being that within a few days of the rebrand the subject of the new logo had been forgotten, along with the platform's old icon.
